metadata.title: What can we learn about teacher support for students from PISA data?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus uses PISA 2022 microdata and reports OECD-average and country/economy estimates for teacher support and related student outcomes. The figures explicitly state that changes are “accounting for students’ and schools’ socio-economic profiles,” implying that analyses control for PISA’s socio-economic profile (ESCS) and use the PISA sampling framework to produce comparable estimates across countries/economies. The document does not report the specific student weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or any replicate-weight method, so the exact weighting and variance-estimation procedure cannot be verified from the excerpt. For replication with the OECD PISA database, analysts should apply the standard PISA complex survey weights and follow the PISA Reader’s Guide/technical documentation for variance estimation; if weights are not applied, cross-country comparisons and statistical significance statements may be unreliable.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This publication is a descriptive policy brief (“PISA in Focus”) that reports associations and changes in indices/percentages using PISA 2022 database tables, rather than training or evaluating an ML model on PV-based achievement outcomes. The excerpt does not document a specific plausible-values strategy (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or a missing-data procedure, so the PV and missing-data handling cannot be verified from the provided text. Given the focus on reporting OECD/PISA database results (e.g., Table B16 and other B tables) without methodological details, this is best treated as a reporting gap for PV/missing-data specifics rather than evidence that PVs are absent.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt does not provide the analytic sample size or explicit inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., grade restriction, school type restriction, or missing-data exclusions). The reported results are based on PISA 2022 participating countries/economies with available data for the specific teacher-support indicators and related student outcomes; charts note that only countries/economies with available data are shown and that an asterisk indicates caution when one or more PISA sampling standards were not met. For the teacher-level analysis, the document states that the teacher questionnaire is optional and that data are available for 18 countries/economies, but it does not specify further filtering criteria.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus synthesizes PISA 2022 evidence on how teacher support in mathematics lessons relates to students’ mathematics performance and well-being, and how teacher support has changed from 2012 to 2022. The brief reports cross-country patterns (e.g., the share of students reporting that teachers continue teaching until students understand) and statistically significant associations between teacher support and outcomes such as mathematics anxiety and “love of learning new things,” with changes accounting for students’ and schools’ socio-economic profiles (ESCS). It also highlights key correlates of teacher support at the student level (quality of student–teacher relationships, disciplinary climate, student persistence) and at the teacher level using PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire data (available for 18 countries/economies), linking teacher time/work-life balance, job satisfaction, and adaptive teaching practices to the learning environment. The document does not provide ML model specifications, PV/missing-data procedures, or weighting/replicate-weight details in the excerpt, so the results should be interpreted as descriptive/associational policy evidence rather than causal estimates.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA in Focus policy brief that reports descriptive and correlational results using precomputed PISA database tables rather than an empirical ML study with a documented predictive pipeline. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV-handling or missing-data strategy described in the excerpt, and no student-level analytic sample sizes reported. The extraction therefore leaves ML-specific fields empty and uses the outcome summary to explain what the PISA indicators and teacher questionnaire analyses cover.
